analysis.one_liner: Limits lawsuits against small-aircraft makers over crashes, replacing state liability rules with a uniform federal standard.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in three House subcommittees until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced state product-liability law for accidents involving small, private aircraft with a single federal set of rules written largely around the defenses available to manufacturers. It would have barred most lawsuits filed more than 20 years after a plane or part was first delivered, no matter when someone was hurt, required victims to file within two years of a crash, allowed punitive damages only under a very high proof standard, and let manufacturers move cases from state courts into federal court. Its stated goal was to cut the liability costs that were shrinking the small-aircraft manufacturing industry.
analysis.who_benefits: General aviation manufacturers — the companies that build small planes, engines, and parts — gain the most, because the bill caps how long they can be sued and raises the bar for punitive damages. Their liability insurers also benefit from fewer and smaller claims. Pilots, aircraft owners, and dealers would face fewer liability claims as well.

how_it_helps.text: It sets a 20-year deadline on lawsuits against manufacturers, counted from when the aircraft or part was first delivered, with only a narrow exception for longer express warranties [S2][S3].
It makes people file suit within two years of an accident and serve the defendant within 120 days, overriding longer or more flexible state deadlines [S2][S3].

It allows punitive damages only if the victim proves by clear and convincing evidence that the maker showed conscious, flagrant indifference to safety, and it blocks evidence of the company's wealth unless that threshold is met first [S2][S3].

It replaces joint liability with several liability in most cases, so a defendant pays only its own percentage share, and it makes a manufacturer's compliance with FAA standards admissible as evidence that its product was not defective [S2][S3].
It lets any defendant remove a crash case from state court to federal court without the victim's consent, and gives federal courts concurrent jurisdiction over claims over $50,000 [S2][S3].
It supersedes any state law on recovery for harm from a general aviation accident wherever the federal rules apply [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed in small-plane crashes and their families would bear the cost: they would lose the right to sue over accidents involving older aircraft, face a hard two-year filing deadline, have a much harder time winning punitive damages, and in many cases be pushed into federal court.

drawbacks.text: The 20-year limit runs from the date an aircraft or part was delivered, not from when harm occurs, so victims hurt by aging aircraft — a large share of the general aviation fleet — could be barred from suing entirely, with only a narrow express-warranty exception [S2][S3].
The two-year filing deadline and 120-day service requirement would override state rules that are often more forgiving, and plaintiffs who miss them lose their claim altogether [S3].
Requiring clear and convincing proof of conscious, flagrant indifference makes punitive damages nearly unreachable, even for serious safety failures short of that standard [S3].

Evidence that a manufacturer complied with FAA standards would be admissible to argue the product was not defective, which could shield designs approved under a certification system that itself missed the danger [S3].
Federal preemption would wipe out stronger state liability protections, and letting any defendant remove cases to federal court adds cost and distance for injured families [S3].

Supporters' own stated concern was real: liability costs and insurance availability were pressuring small-aircraft makers to stop producing some models, and a fair reading of the bill must weigh that against victims' claims [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a genuine benefit — a predictable, uniform liability system aimed at keeping small-aircraft production alive — but its cost falls on the narrowest group in the equation: people hurt or killed in crashes and their families, who would lose claims that current state law allows. The protections for victims it does include (comparative responsibility, several liability with some joint-liability carve-outs, admissibility of tax records to prove lost earnings) soften but do not undo the core effect, which is to shorten, narrow, and federalize the path to compensation.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to three committees, then split among subcommittees, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob McEwen introduced the bill on June 27, 1991, with seven Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Public Works and Transportation committees [S1][S5].

Within three weeks it was split among three subcommittees — Economic and Commercial Law, Aviation, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness — and the Transportation Department was asked for its views [S5].
No further action appears in the record for the rest of the 102nd Congress, which ended January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured in small-plane crashes and their families kept their existing state-law rights to sue, and manufacturers did not get the federal limits on liability they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Crash victims kept their state-law rights

for.name: Rep. Bob McEwen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as a uniform federal liability standard for general aviation accidents.

for.name: General Aviation Manufacturers Association
for.what_they_did: Backed federal product-liability limits for general aviation manufacturers during this period; the industry's campaign later produced the General Aviation Revitalization Act of 1994 with a similar 18-year limit.

against.name: House committee and subcommittee leaders
against.role: Chairs of Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Public Works and Transportation (102nd Congress)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the record shows only referrals to three subcommittees and no further action [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never reached a vote, so no party breakdown of actual support or opposition exists in the record [S4].

industries.note: The bill would cap how long these companies could be sued over crashes, raise the bar for punitive damages, and let them move cases to federal court. The industry had argued liability costs were forcing it to stop producing aircraft, but the savings come directly out of compensation available to crash victims [S2][S3].

Shorter claim windows and harder proof standards mean fewer and smaller payouts for aviation liability policies. Insurers had cited cost and availability problems, but their relief comes at victims' expense [S3].

A 20-year bar, a two-year filing deadline, strict Rule 11 sanctions, and removal to federal court would shrink the pool of viable crash cases these lawyers can bring. Their loss is the mirror of victims' reduced access to court [S2][S3].
